passage:
Internship supervisor's note, week six. Kavitha, analytics team.
Shalini is a careful intern, and her numbers are always right. But she still builds every report by hand in the old spreadsheet, copying data from four files, which takes most of her Thursday. The team moved to the shared dashboard tool a month ago; I showed her once, and she said it looked good. When I asked why she hadn't switched, she smiled. "I'm happy with my way. It works." Then, more quietly: "Learning the new one would take a whole day." She stays late every Thursday.
What I did: I blocked two hours on Monday for us to rebuild one report together in the new tool.

qa.q: How many files does Shalini copy data from?
qa.a: Shalini copies data from four files.

qa.q: What does Shalini's quieter remark about learning the new tool reveal?
qa.a: It reveals that "I'm happy with my way" is partly about avoiding the effort of change; the inertia feels like contentment to her.

qa.q: Why is rebuilding one report together a good step?
qa.a: It makes the switch small and supported, so Shalini can see the time saved without having to find a whole free day alone.

qa.q: How does Kavitha see Shalini's work habits?
qa.a: Kavitha values Shalini's careful, correct numbers but can see the late Thursdays and wants to help her move to a better tool.

grounding: Shows a young adult staying with a slow old method only because switching takes effort, calling it being happy with it.

passage:
Sunday night
Sudha showed me today that she pays half what I do for the same mobile data. Half! My plan is the one Papa set up when I was in Class 9, and I've just... kept it. She sent me the link to switch; it takes about fifteen minutes and a visit to the shop for a new SIM. I said, "Nah, mine's fine, I'm used to it." And I am fine, honestly. It works. But I did the maths on the bus: over a year, the difference would pay for the headphones I keep saying I can't afford. So why haven't I clicked? It's not that I love my plan. I just don't want to do the thing.
Tanvir

qa.q: How long does switching take, according to the link?
qa.a: It takes about fifteen minutes and a visit to the shop for a new SIM.

qa.q: Why does Tanvir say "mine's fine, I'm used to it"?
qa.a: Staying needs no effort, so the old plan feels like a comfortable choice; but Tanvir admits it isn't love for the plan, just not wanting to do the switch.

qa.q: What small step could Tanvir take this week?
qa.a: Tanvir could set aside fifteen minutes to click the link and visit the shop, perhaps with Sudha, so the change feels like one small task.

qa.q: How might Sudha feel when Tanvir says "Nah"?
qa.a: Sudha may feel amused or puzzled, having found an easy saving and watched a friend shrug it off.

grounding: Shows a young adult staying on an overpriced plan only because changing needs effort, and calling the inertia being fine.

passage:
Minakshi: are you still going to that evening coaching for the grad-school entrance test?
Sharmila: yeah. third month
Minakshi: you said the teacher just reads from slides 😅
Sharmila: he does lol. but it's fine. I'm used to the batch
Minakshi: the college prep club is free and the seniors there actually got good scores
Sharmila: I know. but then I'd have to change my whole evening routine, meet new people, figure out the timings…
Minakshi: so you're staying bc switching is annoying?
Sharmila: no! I'm just… content. it's comfy
Minakshi: comfy or stuck? 🤔
Sharmila: …ok that's rude but maybe fair
Sharmila: send me the club timings

qa.q: How long has Sharmila been going to the evening coaching?
qa.a: Sharmila is in the third month of the evening coaching.

qa.q: Why does Sharmila call staying "content" when Minakshi asks?
qa.a: Admitting that the effort of switching is the real reason feels uncomfortable, so Sharmila calls it contentment, though the routine is what keeps Sharmila there.

qa.q: Why is Minakshi's question "comfy or stuck?" helpful?
qa.a: It gently separates real contentment from inertia, which lets Sharmila notice the difference and ask for the club timings.

qa.q: How might Minakshi feel when Sharmila asks for the timings?
qa.a: Minakshi probably feels pleased and relieved that the teasing question landed without hurting the friendship.

grounding: Shows a young adult staying in a weak course only because changing routine takes effort, calling the inertia contentment.

passage: For two years, Ankita had taken the private bus from her town near Karnal to college: forty rupees each way, packed, forty-five minutes of loud film songs. In January a new state bus started on the same route, twenty rupees, half-empty, twenty-five minutes. Her friend Jyoti switched on day one. "Come with me tomorrow," Jyoti said. "No, I'm fine. I know the private bus conductor, I know where to stand. It's comfortable." But Ankita still arrived late and tired every day, and she'd told Jyoti twice that month she was short of money for photocopies. "Comfortable?" Jyoti said. "You complain every day." Ankita laughed. "I'm just used to it." She thought about it that night. Changing meant a new stop, a new timetable, a new conductor. That was all. The next morning she waited at the state bus stop, a little nervous, with Jyoti.

qa.q: How much did the new state bus cost?
qa.a: Twenty rupees.

qa.q: Why did Ankita say she was "fine" on the private bus?
qa.a: It was familiar, and changing felt like effort, a new stop and timetable, so she called her habit comfortable even though she complained daily.

qa.q: What helped Ankita finally switch buses?
qa.a: Thinking it through that night and seeing that changing only meant a new stop, timetable and conductor. Going with Jyoti made the first morning easier.

qa.q: How might Jyoti feel waiting at the state bus stop with Ankita?
qa.a: Jyoti is probably pleased and a bit amused, having watched Ankita complain for weeks while calling it comfortable.

grounding: A young woman keeps taking a slower, costlier bus only because it's familiar, calling it comfortable, until she sees how small the change is.

passage: In Edinburgh, Freya had been paying for a meal-kit subscription since her first term. Every week a box arrived: three recipes, measured spices, a little card. She didn't much like the food, and it cost almost twice what she'd spend at the market. Alejandro, her flatmate, watched her leave half a box of vegetables to wilt again. "Why don't you cancel it?" "It's fine. It's easy," she said. "Is it? You never cook two of the three." Freya shrugged. "Cancelling means logging in, finding the page, answering their 'are you sure' questions. And then I'd have to plan meals." "So you're paying extra to avoid ten minutes." She opened her mouth to argue, then closed it. That evening she found the cancel page. It took seven minutes. On Saturday she and Alejandro walked to the market together, and she bought just what she wanted.

qa.q: How long did it take Freya to cancel the subscription?
qa.a: It took seven minutes.

qa.q: Why did Freya say the subscription was "fine" even though she didn't like it?
qa.a: Cancelling and planning meals felt like effort, so staying felt easier. She called it fine because change seemed like work, not because she was really happy.

qa.q: What turned Freya's thinking around, and what did she do next?
qa.a: Alejandro saying she was paying extra to avoid ten minutes. She found the cancel page that evening and went to the market on Saturday.

qa.q: How might Alejandro feel walking to the market with Freya?
qa.a: Alejandro might feel glad she made the change, and perhaps relieved to stop watching vegetables wilt in their shared fridge. 🙂

grounding: A young woman abroad keeps an overpriced meal-kit subscription only because cancelling feels like effort, until her flatmate points it out.
